newsitem.title: INDIA: India petrochemicals giant aims for global role.
newsitem.headline: India petrochemicals giant aims for global role.

text.p: Petrochemicals and textiles giant Reliance Industries Ltd, India's biggest private firm, is poised to emerge as a global player over the next two years.

"The commissioning of huge capacities will catapult Reliance into the global league, taking its total volume output from 1.6 million tonnes per annum in 1995/96 (April-March) to 6.2 million tonnes in 1997/98," a company spokesman told Reuters.
With further expansion already underway it expects to raise its capacity to 9.3 million tonnes by 1999, he said.

"We like the management's focus and commitment to its chosen businesses and the efforts being made to transform it into a professional petrochemicals company operating on global scales in production capacities," a foreign securities firm said.
Reliance's intrinsic strength helped the firm raise Yankee bonds of 30, 50 and 100-year maturities in the U.S. -- the only Indian firm to have achieved this feat.

The three-decades old company was founded by self-taught entreprenuer Dhirubhai Ambani, 65, who started his career as a gas station assistant. It grew by relentlessly pursuing backward and forward integration -- a strategy that gave it control over every raw material used to make textiles and petrochemicals.

By having all this at each of its two main locations at Patalganga and Hazira in the western states of Maharashtra and Gujarat, it also saved the company transportation, selling, packaging, administrative, remelting and other common costs.

"Projects costing more than 100 billion rupees ($2.79 billion) have gone on stream progressively from September 1996 and will all be commissioned in the span of a year," Jal Irani, petrochemicals analyst at Jardine Fleming, said in a report.
"This will not only result in a tripling in volumes but further enhancement of economies of scale."

When its expansion projects are completed by 1999, it will become the world's second-largest maker of paraxylene with a capacity of 1.58 million tonnes, among the five largest in purified terephthalic acid (PTA) with one million tonnes, and among the fourth biggest for polypropylene with 750,000 tonnes.
It will also be among the 10 biggest makers of bottle grade polyethylene terephthalate, polyvinyl chloride, polyester and polyethylene producers in the world, the company said.

The firm is setting up the world's single largest ethylene cracker, with a capacity to produce 750,000 tonnes a year of thylene, 365,000 tonnes of propylene and more than one million tonnes of by-products.

The polyester, fabric and polymer businesses will be fully integrated from crude oil to branded textiles, making Reliance the only firm to have this degree of integration and capability to capture value addition at all stages, analysts said.

Reliance Petroleum, a group firm, began work last year on a 300,000 barrels per day refinery near the port town of Jamnagar on India's west coast. The 86.94 billion rupees refinery, India's largest, is expected to be commissioned in 2000.
The company's net profits are expected to rise 44 percent in 1997/98 and 46 percent in 1998/99 even though the polyester business may continue to do poorly, Jardine Fleming said.

Its earnings per share (EPS) is forecast to rise 42 percent to 28.89 rupees in 1997/98 and by 40 percent to 39.88 in 1998/99 from 20.10 expected for the year to March 31, 1997, another Hong Kong-based securities firm said.

"We expect a sharp jump in turnover by 62.9 percent in FY (fiscal year) 1998 led by volume increases. We forecast operating margins to remain flat in spite of volume growth, mainly due to the decline in polymer prices," Merrill Lynch said in a December report.
It projected net sales at 126.09 billion rupees for 1997/98 against 77.40 billion in 1996/97, and compared to 62.78 billion in 1995/96.
Pre-tax profit is expected to rise to 14.27 billion rupees in 1996/97 from 13.05 billion a year ago. ($1=35.85 rupees)
